doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First recording with Thad Jones and Billy Mitchell
summary: He describes recording for David Usher's label in a noisy second-floor studio, uneasy with microphones, and the uncertain date.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: When I look at your discography the Thad Jones/Billy Mitchell Quintet it lists at 1953 is that accurate? I haven’t been able to actually find the record.
I don’t think so. You know maybe it was. I don’t know whether that’s correct. You know the Bluebird is still there! I could call ‘em up and ask them to look it up in the book! (Laughs)
But was that your first recording with Thad Jones and Billy Mitchell?
Yeah with Thad and Big Billy Mitchell, yeah.
What was that like making your first recording?
It was like nothing you ever saw in your life! (Laughs).
Could you please describe what that means? (Laughs)
I don’t know what the engineer was doing! (Laughs) That was some funny stuff.
So how did it come about that there was that recording? Did somebody come along and say, “Hey I want to record you guys or was there…”
No, you know there was this guy and his name was David Usher. And he had a—he was a good friend of Dizzy. And as a matter of fact Dizzy had a label called D.G.
Remember that yellow label? He wanted to record Billy and our band out there on that label. That’s what happened.
So you went into the recording studio, of course you had to bring your drums. How was the recording studio? Was it a makeshift studio or was it a bona fide studio?

It looked more like this room than anything else. (Laughs). It was on the 2nd story of this building and it was right next to this fire-dock where the cars were going (imitates loud car’s growling) and you could hear it!
Do you remember the session going smoothly?

Yeah we just played what we would play at the club. Sometimes—it’s different because recording, you’re not playing for anybody particularly. It’s just like a performance for the air. I think that’s kind of scary. I couldn’t understand what they were going to do. I said, “What are you going to do with this?” Cause it didn’t sound right to me. I wasn’t comfortable but you learn. That was the first recording I ever tried so I learned a log.
Do you remember what it was like hearing yourself on the playback and what did you think?

Well you know I couldn’t hear it that very well. It wasn’t mixed. It was bad reception. I didn’t think it was recorded so good. The record is out someplace and somebody’s got it. I’d like to have a copy of it myself.
So I think what I’ll do is go to the Institute of Jazz Studies at Rutgers and I’ll see if I can get a copy I’ll get you a copy.
Oh, okay yeah. That’d be great.
Yeah cause you should have that.
Thank you.
Sure. Let’s take a break.
Sure. (Anthony Brown, Ken Kimery, Elvin Jones, and Keiko take a break. The question asked, which Elvin is heard responding to, is not recorded)
